Tags & a few honest questions (click to open)
cheapestThe lowest-price pack in that table.
⚠️ failed batchesGovernment-lab batches of that medicine by that maker that failed testing (Jan 2019 – Sep 2026). A failed batch is that batch — not every batch of the brand.
discontinuedAn old pack that may no longer be in shops — always listed last. Status is tracked for the leading makers; for other makers a pack shows as current simply because their status is not published.
trust scoreThe maker’s points (0–100) from public regulatory records only — FDA warning letters, import alerts, recalls. 70+ = clean record; “not rated” = no public record found, never invented.
Global research companyBayer, Pfizer, GSK, Haleon, Abbott, Novartis, Sanofi… — the Indian arm of a global researcher.
🍫 chemist-stapleOne of the ~100 most-stocked Indian brands (Crocin, Dolo, Augmentin…). Chemists keep them or can order them from their distributor in 1–2 days — a substitute being pushed is about margins, not availability.
Table order: most maker points first → within the top score: the cheaper pack first → below it: fewest failed batches, then price. अ at the top right switches the interface to Hindi.
Are the prices live?
While you are online, prices re-check themselves as you search (PharmEasy live) and the owner’s verified updates arrive automatically. Fully offline you see the last saved prices — always confirm the current MRP on the pack at the pharmacy.
What is behind each price I see?
Every price carries an honest source and date: NPPA ceiling (the legal maximum for scheduled formulations, nppa.gov.in) · Jan Aushadhi (government generic shelf price, pmbi.co.in) · live re-check (PharmEasy real MRP, with its date) · catalog snapshot (inherited MRP with its date) · user report (what a person actually paid — unverified until re-checked). A weekly pipeline moves rows out of “snapshot” into dated sources over time.
The chemist says my brand is not available and pushes a substitute — is that real?
Usually no. Chemists stock or can order every well-known brand (look for the 🍫 chemist-staple tag); substitutes get pushed because margins differ, not because the 85-scored brand is unavailable. Any chemist can order any brand from their distributor in 1–2 days — ask, and show the name from the app. Online pharmacies (1mg, PharmEasy, Apollo) stock them all and often sell below MRP — the app deep-links each store’s live search. For the salt itself, a Jan Aushadhi kendra is the cheapest legitimate option (18,646 kendras, CDSCO-audited quality) — medicine pages with a matching generic show the kendra price.
Is a trust score of 85 required?
No — it is one input, not a bar. Serum Institute 75, Dr. Reddy’s 75, Lupin 74, Mankind 72, Aristo 72, Eris/Macleods/Cadila 70 are all solid; “not rated” means no public international record was found, never “bad”. Availability and price are the other two inputs — an in-stock 70 that is half the price beats a back-ordered 85 for most people.
Why keep the lower-scored makers?
Only 28 of 74 makers score 70+. Removing the rest would leave 43% of salt-and-strength searches with nothing to show, and the 70+ option is often the dearer one. Their packs are licensed, batch-tested and legal — the score is printed so the choice stays yours.
Is my strip’s batch flagged by the government?
Tools → CDSCO batch checker — type the batch number from any strip in your hand.
Is this medical advice?
No — it is a shopping guide built from public records and standard published references. The doctor’s prescription stays the authority; ask your doctor or chemist before choosing or changing anything.
PS Medico lists 52,541 products from the leading makers as alternatives (old packs marked “discontinued” may no longer be in shops). The search box also finds any of 262,303 medicine listings (every medicine and every pack size) from the public Indian-medicine catalog (github.com/junioralive/Indian-Medicine-Dataset, a Tata 1mg-derived snapshot) so you can look up any company's brand — each with its maker’s trust score; alternatives are shown only from those leading makers. Maker trust scores come from public regulatory records only (FDA warning letters, import alerts, recalls) — no paid rankings. Uses and common side effects are in plain words (medical term in brackets); banned or withdrawn drugs are flagged. When you are online, prices re-check themselves while you search and unknown medicines are found on the internet and added automatically. Prices are from the catalog snapshot, not live — this file works fully offline, so check the current MRP at your pharmacy. Not medical advice.
